nodes.name: Weighted graph and weighted adjacency matrix
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}, \mathrm{W})$  be a directed, irregular and weighted graph, where $\mathcal{V} = \{v_i \}_{i=1}^N$ is the set of nodes, $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of weighted edges, and $\mathrm{W} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, whose element $\mathrm{W}_{i,j}$ measures the underlying relation between the $i$th and the $j$th nodes.

nodes.name: Degree vector
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{d} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$ be a degree vector, where $d_i = \sum_j \mathrm{W}_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Graph signal
nodes.statement:
Given a fixed ordering of nodes, we assign a signal coefficient to each node; a~\emph{graph signal} is then defined as a vector,
$$
	\mathbf{x} = [x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_N]^T \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N,
$$
with $x_n$ the signal coefficient corresponding to the node $v_n$.

nodes.name: Graph shift operator
nodes.statement: We use the graph shift operator $\mathrm{A} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ as a graph representation, which is an elementary filtering operation that replaces a signal coefficient at a node with a weighted linear combination of coefficients at its neighboring nodes.
differentia: replaces a signal coefficient at a node with a weighted linear combination of coefficients at its neighboring nodes

nodes.name: Normalized adjacency matrix and transition matrix
nodes.statement: Some common choices of a graph shift are weighted adjacency matrix $\mathrm{W}$, normalized adjacency matrix $\mathrm{W}_{\rm norm} = {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{W} {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and transition matrix $\mathrm{P} = {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-1} \mathrm{W}$~\cite{ChenSMK:13}.

nodes.name: Graph Laplacian matrix
nodes.statement: The second one is based on the spectral graph theory~\cite{Chung:96}, where the graph Laplacian matrix $\mathrm{L} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ is used  as a graph representation, which is a second-order difference operator on graphs.

nodes.name: Unnormalized, normalized and transition Laplacians
nodes.statement: Some common choices of a graph Laplacian matrix are the unnormalized Laplacian  ${\rm diag}(\mathbf{d}) - \mathrm{W}$, the normalized Laplacian  $\mathrm{I} - {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}} \mathrm{W} {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, and the transition Laplacian $\mathrm{I} - {\rm diag}(\mathbf{d})^{-1} \mathrm{W} $.

nodes.name: Graph structure matrix
nodes.statement: We use $\mathrm{R} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{N \times N}$ to represent a graph structure matrix, which can be either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix.
differentia: either a graph shift or a graph Laplacian matrix

nodes.name: Graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement_short: The graph Fourier basis V is the eigenvector matrix of R = V Lambda V^{-1}; its columns are graph Fourier basis vectors.

nodes.name: Graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
The graph Fourier transform \rm{of $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N$} is 
$
	\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathrm{U} \mathbf{x},
$
where $\mathrm{U} = \mathrm{V}^{-1}$ is called the graph Fourier transform matrix.

nodes.name: Inverse graph Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
The~\textit{inverse graph Fourier transform} is
$
	\mathbf{x} =  \mathrm{V}  \widehat{\mathbf{x}}.
$

nodes.name: Variation with respect to a graph shift
Graph shift eigenvalue order gives variation order
nodes.statement: We can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\mathrm{A} $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order $\lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_1 \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_2 \geq \ldots \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{A})}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{A}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_1) \leq \mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{A})}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{A})}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{A})}_N)$.
assumptions: the eigenvalues of the graph shift $\mathrm{A} $ are sorted in a nonincreasing order
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follow a nondecreasing order
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvectors of a graph shift with decreasing eigenvalues have increasing variation.

nodes.name: Variation with respect to a graph Laplacian
nodes.statement:
When the graph representation matrix is the graph Laplacian matrix, the variation of a graph signal $\mathbf{x}$ is defined as,
 \begin{equation*} 	\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}} (\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i,j=1}^N \mathrm{A}_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2 = \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x}. \end{equation*}

nodes.name: Graph Laplacian eigenvalue order gives variation order
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that when the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\mathrm{L}$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order $\lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_1 \leq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_2 \leq \ldots \leq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_N$, the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_1) \leq \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_2) \leq \ldots \leq \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{L}}(\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_N)$.
assumptions: the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian $\mathrm{L}$ are sorted in a nondecreasing order
conclusions: the variations of the corresponding eigenvectors follows a nondecreasing order

nodes.name: Low-frequency and high-frequency components
nodes.statement: The variations of graph Fourier basis vectors thus allow us to provide the ordering:  the Fourier basis vectors with small variations are considered as \textit{low-frequency} components while the vectors with large variations are considered as \textit{high-frequency} components~\cite{SandryhailaM:131}.

nodes.name: Graph Fourier bases ordered from low to high frequency
nodes.statement: In the following discussion, we assume all graph Fourier bases are ordered from low frequencies to high frequencies.

nodes.name: Descriptive graph signal model
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal, $f(\cdot)$ be a function operating on $\mathbf{x}$, we define a class of graph signals by restricting
\begin{equation} f(\mathbf{x})  \leq C,
\end{equation}
where $C$ is some constant.
nodes.statement_short: A class of graph signals is defined by bounding an operator output: f(x) <= C.

nodes.name: Descriptive model constraint
nodes.statement: f(\mathbf{x})  \leq C,
nodes.label: eq:descriptive

Sparse coding problem
nodes.statement:
We consider approximating a graph signal by using a linear combination of a few atoms from $\mathrm{D}$ and solving the following sparse coding problem,
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{a}^*=  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{a}} & d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x} ),
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} & \mathbf{x}' = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a}, 
   \\
   \nonumber
   && \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K.
\end{eqnarray}
where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate x by D a with at most K nonzero coefficients, minimizing a metric d(x', x).

nodes.name: Sparse coding formulation
nodes.statement:
\mathbf{x}^*, \mathbf{a}^*=  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{a}} & d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x} ),
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} & \mathbf{x}' = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a}, 
   \\
   \nonumber
   && \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K.
nodes.label: eq:sparse_coding

nodes.name: Sampling operator
nodes.statement_short: The sampling operator is Psi = C F, where C selects M rows of a sampling pattern matrix F.

nodes.name: Sampling operator
nodes.statement: \Psi = \mathrm{C} \mathrm{F} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{M \times N},
nodes.label: eq:Psi

nodes.name: Row-selection matrix C
nodes.label: eq:C

nodes.name: Uniform, experimentally designed and active sampling
nodes.statement: There are three sampling strategies: (1) uniform sampling when designing $\mathrm{C}$, , where row indices are chosen from from $\{0, 1, \cdots, N-1\}$ independently and uniformly; and~\emph{experimentally design sampling}, where row indices can be chosen beforehand; and~\emph{active sampling}, where we will use feedback as samples are sequentially collected to decide the next row to be sampled.

nodes.name: Subsampling and compressed sampling operators
nodes.statement: The sampling pattern matrix $\mathrm{F}$ constraints the following sampling patterns: when $\mathrm{F}$ is an identity matrix, $\Psi$ is a subsampling operator; when $\mathrm{F}$ is a Gaussian random matrix,  $\Psi$ is a compressed sampling operator.

nodes.name: Noisy samples
nodes.statement:
In the sampling phase, we take
samples with the sampling operator $\Psi$,
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{x}_{\Psi} = \Psi \mathbf{y} = \Psi ( \mathbf{x}  + \epsilon),
\end{equation*}
 is a vector of samples and $\epsilon$ is
noise with zero mean and $\sigma^2$ as variance.

nodes.name: Recovery operator
nodes.statement:
In the recovery phase, we
reconstruct the graph signal by using a recovery operator $\Phi$, 
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{x}' = \Phi \mathbf{x}_{\Psi},
\end{equation*}
where $\mathbf{x}'$ recovers $\mathbf{x}$ either
exactly or approximately.

nodes.name: Optimal sampling and recovery design
nodes.statement:
The prototype of designing sampling and recovery strategies is
\begin{eqnarray*}
\Psi^*(\mathrm{D}), \Phi^*(\mathrm{D}) = \min_{\Psi, \Phi} \max_{\mathbf{a}} && d(\mathbf{x}', \mathbf{x}),
\\
 {\rm subject~to} && \mathbf{x}' = \Phi \Psi (\mathbf{x} + \epsilon),
\\
&& \mathbf{x} = \mathrm{D} \mathbf{a},
\end{eqnarray*}
where $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is some evaluation metric.
nodes.statement_short: Min-max design of sampling Psi and recovery Phi for signals x = D a under noise.

nodes.name: Atoms of a dictionary
nodes.statement:
The columns of $\mathrm{D}_{K}$ are denoted as $\mathrm{D}^{(k)}$, $k
= 0, \ldots, K$, and called \emph{atoms}; the elements of each atom
$\mathrm{D}^{(k)}$ are $n^k$.

nodes.name: Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschitz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf Graph polynomial dictionary represents the pairwise Lipschiz smooth signals}) $\mathrm{PL}(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{PL}(1)$ is a subset of the pairwise Lipschitz smooth with some parameter $C$.
nodes.label: thm:BLvsGS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PL}(1)$, that is,
$$
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}
	{\bf 1}  &  \mathrm{D}^{(1)}  
	\end{bmatrix} \mathbf{a},
$$
Then, we write the pairwise Lipschitz smooth criterion as
\begin{eqnarray*}
|x_i - x_j| 
& = &  | \sum_{k} \left( d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) \right)   a_k |
\\
& \leq &  \sum_{k} | d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) |  |a_k |
\\
\\
& \leq &  \sum_{k} |a_k |  | d(v_i, v_j) | \ = \ \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_1  | d(v_i, v_j) |.
\end{eqnarray*}
The parameter $C = \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_1$, which corresponds to the energy of the original graph signal.
nodes.statement_short: Direct bound via the triangle inequality for the distance, giving C = ||a||_1.

nodes.name: Bandlimited graph signal
Graph Fourier bases V_L, V_P, V_W
nodes.statement: When $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the unnormalized graph Laplacian matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ are total Lipschitz smooth; when $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the transition matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ are local normalized neighboring smooth; when $\mathrm{V}$ is the eigenvector matrix of the weighted adjacency matrix, we denote it as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$ and can show that signals in $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ are global normalized neighboring smooth.
nodes.statement_short: V_L, V_P, V_W denote the eigenvector matrices of the Laplacian, transition and adjacency matrices.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschitz smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian represents the total Lipschiz smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_k$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}(K)$ is a subset of the total Lipschitz smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:BLvsGS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is,
$$
\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k,
$$
Then, we write the total Lipschitz smooth criterion as
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} ( x_i - x_j )^2 
\ = \ \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} 
\\
& =  &  (\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k)^T (\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k \lambda_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{L})}_k)
\ = \   \sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_k \widehat{x}_k^2 
\\
& \leq & \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_K   \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k^2  
\ = \   \lambda^{(\mathrm{L})}_K.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand x in Laplacian eigenvectors; x^T L x = sum lambda_k xhat_k^2 <= lambda_K.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the transition matrix represents the local normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})^2$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{P}}}(K)$ is a subset of the local normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:LNNS

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is,
$$
\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k,
$$
Then, we write the local normalized neighboring smooth criterion as

\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \left| x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} }  \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j  \right|
\\
&= &   \left| \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_i - \sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_j \right|
\\
& = &   \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \left(  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_j \right) \right|
\\
& = &   \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k  (1 - \lambda_k)  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i \right|
\\
& \leq &  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})  \left| \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i  \right| \ = \  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})  |x_i|.
\end{eqnarray*}
The last equality follows from the fact that $\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ and $\lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\mathrm{P}$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \sum_i \left(  x_i -  \frac{1}{\sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i }}  \sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i } \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j  \right)^2 
\\
& = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} }  \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j |^2
\\
& \leq & \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}   (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K} )^2  |x_i|^2 \ = \   (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})^2 .
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand in eigenvectors of P; pointwise bound by (1 - lambda_K)|x_i|, then sum squares.

nodes.name: The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals
nodes.statement: ({\bf The graph Fourier basis of the adjacency matrix represents the global normalized neighboring smooth signals}) For any $K \in \{1, \cdots, N \}$, $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$, when $C \geq  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{W})}_{K} / |\lambda_{\max}{(\mathrm{W})}| )^2$.
conclusions: $\mathrm{BL}_{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}}(K)$ is a subset of the global normalized neighboring smooth with parameter $C$
nodes.label: thm:GNNS

nodes.name: Frame bounds of smooth-signal dictionaries
nodes.statement: \mypar{Frame Bound} Graph polynomial dictionary is highly redundant and the frame bound is loose. When the graph is undirected, the adjacency matrix is symmetric, then $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{W}}$ are orthonormal. It is hard to draw any meaningful conclusion when the graph is directed; we leave it for the future work.

nodes.name: Sparse representations of smooth-signal dictionaries
nodes.statement: \mypar{Sparse Representations} Graph polynomial dictionary provides sparse representations for polynomial graph signals. On the other hand, the graph Fourier bases provide sparse representations for the bandlimited graph signals. For approximately bandlimited graph signals, there are some residuals coming from the high-frequency components.

nodes.name: Localization possible on irregular graphs
nodes.statement: We see that the lower bound involves with the maximum magnitude of $\mathrm{U}_{\Omega}$. In classical signal processing, $\mathrm{U}$ is the discrete Fourier transform matrix, so $\left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}  = 1/\sqrt{N}$; the lower bound is $O(N)$ and signals cannot localize in both time and frequency domain. However, for complex and irregular graphs, the energy of a graph Fourier basis vector may concentrate on a few elements, that is, $\left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty} = O(1)$, as shown in Figures~\ref{fig:geo_fourier}(a)(b)(c)(d). It is thus possible that  graph signals can be localized in both the vertex and spectrum domain.
nodes.statement_short: Unlike the DFT case, graph Fourier vectors can concentrate, so signals may localize in both vertex and spectrum domains.

nodes.name: Localization of a graph signal
nodes.statement: The \textit{localization} of a graph signal means that most elements in a graph signal are zeros, or have small values; only a small number of elements have large magnitudes and the corresponding nodes are clustered in one subgraph with a small diameter.

nodes.name: Inverse participation ratio (IPR)
Energy concentration ratio (ECR)
nodes.statement:
We use \textit{energy concentration ratio} (ECR) to quantify the energy concentration property. The ECR is defined as 
\begin{equation*}
\rm{ECR} = \frac{S^*}{N},
\end{equation*}
where $S^*$ is the smallest $S$ that satisfies
$
\left\| \mathbf{x}_S \right\|_2^2 \geq 95\%  \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2,
$
with $\mathbf{x}_S$ the first $S$ elements with the largest magnitude in $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: ECR = S*/N, the smallest fraction of largest-magnitude entries holding 95% of the energy.

nodes.name: Normalized geodesic distance (NGD)
nodes.statement_short: NGD is the average pairwise geodesic distance among nodes holding 95% of the energy, divided by the diameter.

nodes.name: Localized graph Fourier basis
nodes.statement: Each graph Fourier basis vector is regarded as a graph signal. When most basis vectors in the graph Fourier basis are localized, that is, the corresponding ECRs and NGDs are small, we call that graph Fourier basis localized.

nodes.name: Graph Fourier bases of real networks are localized
nodes.statement: We find that a large number of graph Fourier basis vectors has small ECRs and NGDs, which indicates that graph Fourier basis vectors of various graph representation matrices are localized.

nodes.name: Nonlinear approximation
nodes.statement:
Let $\{ \phi_k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N \}_{k=1}^N$ and  $\{ \widehat{\phi}_k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N \}_{k=1}^N$ be a pair of biorthonormal basis and $\mathbf{x} \in  \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N $ be a signal. Here the graph Fourier transform matrix $\mathrm{U} = \{ \widehat{\phi}_k \}_{k=1}^N$ and the graph Fourier basis $\mathrm{V} = \{ \phi_k \}_{k=1}^N$. The nonlinear approximation to $\mathbf{x}$ is 
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\mathbf{x}, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k,
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathcal{I}_K$ is the index set of the $K$ largest-magnitude expansion coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Keep the K largest-magnitude expansion coefficients in a biorthonormal basis.

nodes.name: Nonlinear approximation
nodes.statement: \mathbf{x}^* = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_K} \left\langle {\mathbf{x}, \widehat{\phi}_k} \right\rangle \phi_k,
nodes.label: eq:nonlinear_approx

nodes.name: Sparse coding with the graph polynomial dictionary
nodes.statement:
Since the the graph polynomial dictionary is redundant, we solve the following sparse coding problem,
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{x}^* =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)} \mathbf{a}  \right\|_2^2,
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} &  \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)}$ is the graph polynomial dictionary with order $2$ and $\mathbf{a}$ are expansion coefficients.

nodes.name: l2 sparse coding with D_poly(2)
nodes.statement:
\mathbf{x}^* =  &  \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}} & \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm poly(2)} \mathbf{a}  \right\|_2^2,
   \\
   \nonumber
   & {\rm subject~to:~} &  \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq K,
nodes.label: eq:l2_sparse_coding

nodes.name: Normalized mean square error
nodes.statement:
To make a more serious comparison, we evaluate the approximation error by using the normalized mean square error, that is,
\begin{equation} {\rm Normalized~MSE} = \frac{ \left\|  \mathbf{x}^* - \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 }{ \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 },
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{x}^*$ is the approximation signal and $\mathbf{x}$ is the original signal.

nodes.name: Normalized MSE
nodes.statement: {\rm Normalized~MSE} = \frac{ \left\|  \mathbf{x}^* - \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 }{ \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 },
nodes.label: eq:NMSE

nodes.name: Expansion coefficients concentrated on a known support
nodes.statement: In general, we assume that the energy of the expansion coefficient $\mathbf{a}$ is concentrated in a few known supports, that is, $\left\| \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} \right\|_2 \gg \left\| \mathbf{a}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2$, where $|\Omega| \ll N $ and $\Omega$ is the known.

nodes.name: Partial least squares recovery
nodes.statement:
We consider the partial least squares (PLS), $x^*_{\rm PLS}  \ = \  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}  \mathbf{a}^*_{\rm PLS} $, where
\begin{eqnarray} \mathbf{a}^*_{\rm PLS}  & = & 	
	  \arg \min_{ \mathbf{a}}  \left\|  \Psi^T \mathbf{x}_{\Psi} -  \Psi^T \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} \right\|_2^2
	\nonumber
	\\
	& = &   \left(  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \Psi^T \Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \right)^{-1}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \Psi^T \Psi \mathbf{y}
	\nonumber
	\\
	\nonumber
	& = & (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi ( \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} + \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega^c}  + \epsilon ),
\end{eqnarray}
where $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \epsilon$ is the noisy version of the graph signal with $\epsilon$ is noise, $(\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi = \left(  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \mathrm{S}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \right)^{-1}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \mathrm{S}$ and $\mathrm{S} =  \Psi^T \Psi$, which is a diagonal matrix with $\mathrm{S}_{i,i}= 1$, when the $i$th node is sampled, and 0, otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: PLS recovers a_Omega by least squares on the samples: a* = (Psi D_Omega)^dagger Psi y.

nodes.name: Partial least squares
nodes.statement:
\mathbf{a}^*_{\rm PLS}  & = & 	
	  \arg \min_{ \mathbf{a}}  \left\|  \Psi^T \mathbf{x}_{\Psi} -  \Psi^T \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} \right\|_2^2
	\nonumber
	\\
	& = &   \left(  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega}^T \Psi^T \Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \right)^{-1}  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \Psi^T \Psi \mathbf{y}
	\nonumber
	\\
	\nonumber
	& = & (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi ( \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega} + \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \mathbf{a}_{\Omega^c}  + \epsilon ),
nodes.label: eq:PLS

nodes.name: Recovery error decomposition of PLS
Optimal sampling operator design (six settings)
nodes.statement:
We aim to optimize the sampling strategy by minimizing the recovery error and there are six cases to be considered: 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item minimizing the bias in the worst case; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2,
	$$
	where $ \sigma_{\max}$ is the largest singular value;
	\item minimizing the bias in expectation; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{S}   \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi   \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_{F}^2,
	$$
	where $\left\| \cdot \right\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm;
	\item minimizing the variance from noise in the worst case; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_2;
	$$
	\item minimizing the variance from noise in expectation; that is,	
	$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_F;
	$$
	\item minimizing the recovery error in worst case, that is,
$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_2	+ c \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_2,
$$
	where $c$ is related to the signal-to-noise ratio;
	\item minimizing the recovery error in expectation; that is,
$$
	\min_{\Psi}  \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \mathrm{D}_{\Omega^c} \right\|_F + c \left\| (\Psi \mathrm{D}_{\Omega} )^{\dagger} \Psi  \right\|_F,
$$
	where $c$ is related to the signal-to-noise ratio.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Choose Psi minimizing PLS bias, noise variance or both, in worst case or expectation.

nodes.name: Optimal sampling operator
nodes.statement: We call the resulting sampling operator $\Psi$ of each setting as an~\emph{optimal sampling operator with respect to setting ($\cdot$)}.
nodes.definiendum: optimal sampling operator with respect to setting ($\cdot$)

nodes.name: Graph difference operator
nodes.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be the~\emph{graph difference
  operator} (the oriented incidence matrix of $G$), whose rows
correspond to edges~\cite{SharpnackRS:12, WangSST:15}. For example, if
$e_i$ is a directed edge that connects the $j$th node to the $k$th
node ($j < k$), the elements of the $i$th row of $\Delta$ are
\begin{equation*} \Delta_{i, \ell} = 
  \left\{ 
    \begin{array}{rl}
      - {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = j;\\
       {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = k;\\
      0, & \mbox{otherwise},
  \end{array} \right.
\end{equation*}
where $\mathrm{W}$ is the weighted adjacency matrix, sgn$(\cdot)$ denotes the sign, which is used to handle the negative edge weights.
nodes.origin_citation: Sharpnack, Rinaldo, Singh 2012; Wang, Sharpnack, Smola, Tibshirani 2015
nodes.statement_short: Delta is the signed, weight-scaled oriented incidence matrix with one row per edge.

nodes.name: Graph difference operator entries
nodes.statement:
\Delta_{i, \ell} = 
  \left\{ 
    \begin{array}{rl}
      - {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = j;\\
       {\rm sgn}(\mathrm{W}_{j,k}) \sqrt{ | \mathrm{W}_{j,k} | }, & \ell = k;\\
      0, & \mbox{otherwise},
  \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:Delta

nodes.name: Edge signal
nodes.statement: The graph difference operator compares the signal coefficients of two nodes connected by each edge and $\Delta \mathbf{x}$ is an~\emph{edge signal} representing the difference of $\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Difference operator norm equals Laplacian quadratic form
nodes.statement: When $G$ is an undirected graph, $\left\| \Delta \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 = \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x}$, where $\mathrm{L}$ is the graph Laplacian matrix, which measures the total Lipschiz smoothness as shown in Definition~\ref{df:global_Lip}.

nodes.name: Difference operator of an unweighted graph
assumptions: When the graph is unweighted and all the edge weights are nonnegative

nodes.name: Unweighted difference operator entries
nodes.statement:
\Delta_{i, \ell} = 
  \left\{ 
    \begin{array}{rl}
      1, & \ell = k;  \\
      -1, & \ell = j; \\
      0, & \mbox{otherwise}.
  \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:C

nodes.statement: Each element of $\Delta \mathbf{x}$ is the difference between two adjacenct signal coefficient; when $\left( \Delta \mathbf{x} \right)_i \neq 0$, we call the $i$th edge is inconsistent.

nodes.statement: The class $\mathrm{PC}_{G}(K)$ represents signals that contain at most $K$ inconsistent edges.

nodes.name: Local sets
nodes.statement: Let $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$ be the partition of the node set $\mathcal{V}$. We call $\{S_c\}_{c=1}^C$~\emph{local sets} when they satisfy that the subgraph corresponding to each local set is connected, that is, when $G_{S_c}$ is connected for all $c$.
differentia: the subgraph corresponding to each local set is connected
nodes.label: df:localset

nodes.name: Local-set-based graph signal
Normalized variation of a local set
nodes.statement:
For a local-set-based graph signal, we measure its smoothness by the normalized variation
$$
\mathrm{S}_{\Delta, p} (S) = \frac{1}{\left\|  {\bf 1}_S  \right\|_p^p}\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_S \right\|_p^p.
$$

nodes.name: Piecewise-constant graph signal based on local sets
nodes.label: df:pc_gen

nodes.name: General multiresolution analysis on graphs
nodes.statement_short: Nested subspaces V_0 in ... in V_K whose union is R^N, intersection the constants, with an orthonormal basis.
nodes.label: df:MRA

nodes.name: Local set decomposition tree construction
nodes.statement:
We initialize $S_{0,1} = \mathcal{V}$
to correspond to the $0$th level subspace $V_0$, that is, $V_0 = \{
c_0 {\bf 1}_{S_{0,1}}, c_0 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. We then partition $S_{0,1}$
into two disjoint local sets $S_{1,1}$ and $S_{1,2}$, corresponding to the first level subspace $V_1$, where $V_1 = \{ c_1 {\bf 1}_{S_{1,1}}
+ c_2 {\bf 1}_{S_{1,2}}, c_1, c_2 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. We then
recursively partition each larger local set into two smaller local
sets. For the $i$th level subspace, we have $V_i = \sum_{j=1}^{2^i}
c_j {\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}}$ and then, we partition $S_{i,j}$ into
$S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ for all $j = 1, 2, \ldots, 2^i$.  We call
$S_{i,j}$ the parent set of $S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ and
$S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ are the children sets of $S_{i,j}$. When
$|S_{i,j}| \leq 1$, $S_{i+1,2j-1} = S_{i,j}$ and $S_{i+1,2j} =
\emptyset$. At the finest resolution, each local set corresponds to an
individual node or an empty set. In other words, we build a binary
decomposition tree that partitions a graph structure into multiple
local sets.
nodes.statement_short: Recursively bipartition local sets into connected children, building a binary decomposition tree down to single nodes.

nodes.name: Parent and children local sets
nodes.statement:
We call
$S_{i,j}$ the parent set of $S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ and
$S_{i+1,2j-1}, S_{i+1,2j}$ are the children sets of $S_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Depth of the decomposition
nodes.statement:
The $i$th level of the decomposition tree corresponds to
the $i$th level subspace. The depth of the decomposition $T$
depends on how local sets are partitioned; $T$ ranges from
$N$ to $\ceil*{\log N}$, where $N$ corresponds to partitioning one
node at a time and $\ceil*{\log N}$ corresponds to an even partition
at each level.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6 (in prose)
nodes.statement:
It is clear that the proposed construction of local sets satisfies three requirements in Definition~\ref{df:MRA}. The initial subspace $V_0$ has the coast resolution. Through partitioning, local sets zoom into
increasingly finer resolutions in the graph vertex domain. The subspace $V_T$ with finest resolution zoom into each individual node and covers the entire $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$.  Classical scale invariance requires that when $f(t) \in V_0$, then $f(2^m t) \in V_m$, which is ill-posed
in the graph domain because graphs are finite and discrete;
the classical translation invariance requires that when $f(t) \in
V_0$, then $f(t-n) \in V_0$, which is again ill-posed, this time
because graphs are irregular. The essence of scaling and translation
invariance, however, is to use the same function and its scales and
translates to span different subspaces, which is what the proposed
construction promotes. The scaling function is ${\bf 1}_{S}$; the hierarchy of partition is similar to the scaling and translation, that is, when ${\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i}$, then ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j-1}}, {\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$, and when ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j-1}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$ then ${\bf 1}_{S_{i+1,2j}} \in \mathcal{V}_{i+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check upward/downward completeness and basis existence directly from the recursive partition.

nodes.name: Local set decomposition tree on four nodes
nodes.statement: We now show a toy example in Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition}. In Partition 1, we partition the entire node set $S_{0,1} = \mathcal{V} = \{1, 2, 3, 4 \}$ into two disjoint local sets $S_{1,1} =  \{1, 2 \}, S_{1,2} =  \{3, 4 \}$. Thus, $V_1 = \{ c_1  {\bf 1_{S_{1,1}}} +  c_2  {\bf 1_{S_{1,2}}}  , c_1, c_2 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \}$. Similarly, in Partition 2, we partition $S_{1,1}$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_{2,1} =  \{1 \}, S_{2,2}  =  \{ 2 \}$; in Partition 3, we partition $S_{1,2}$ into $S_{2,3}  =  \{3 \}, S_{2,4}  =  \{ 4 \}$. Thus, $V_2 = \{ c_1  {\bf 1_{S_{2,1}}} +  c_2  {\bf 1_{S_{2,2}}} + c_3 {\bf 1_{S_{2,3}}} +  c_4  {\bf 1_{S_{2,4}}} , c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4 \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}} \} = \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^4$.

nodes.name: Graph partition problem for local sets
nodes.statement:
From the perspective of promoting smoothness of graph signals, we partition a local set $S$ into two disjoint local set $S_1, S_2$ by solving the following optimization problem
\begin{eqnarray} & \min_{S_1, S_2} & \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_1) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_2)
\\
\nonumber
& {\rm subject~to:} & S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset, S_1 \cup S_2 = S, 
\\
\nonumber
&& G_{S_1}~{\rm and}~G_{S_2}  {\rm~are~connected}.
\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Split a local set into two connected parts minimizing the sum of their normalized variations.

nodes.name: Graph partition objective
nodes.statement:
& \min_{S_1, S_2} & \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_1) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_2)
\\
\nonumber
& {\rm subject~to:} & S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset, S_1 \cup S_2 = S, 
\\
\nonumber
&& G_{S_1}~{\rm and}~G_{S_2}  {\rm~are~connected}.
nodes.label: algo:partition

nodes.name: Spectral clustering partition
nodes.statement: The first one is based on spectral clustering~\cite{Luxburg:07}. We first obtain the graph Laplacian matrix of a local set and compute the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian matrix. We then set the median number of the eigenvector as the threshold; we put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are no smaller than the threshold into a children local set and put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are smaller than the threshold into the other children local set.
nodes.statement_short: Split a local set at the median of the Fiedler vector of its Laplacian.

nodes.name: Spanning tree partition
nodes.statement: The second one is based on spanning tree. To partition a local set, we first obtain the maximum spanning tree of the subgraph and then find a balance node in the spanning tree. The balance node partition the spanning tree into two subtrees with the closet number of nodes~\cite{SharpnackKS:13}. We remove the balance node from the spanning tree, the resulting largest connected component form a children local set and the other nodes including the balance node forms the other children local set.
nodes.statement_short: Split at a balance node of the maximum spanning tree.

nodes.name: 2-means partition
nodes.statement: The third one is based on the 2-means clustering. We first randomly select 2 nodes as the community center and assign every other node to its nearest community center based on the geodesic distance. We then recompute the community center for each community by minimizing the summation of the geodesic distances to all the other nodes in the community and assign node to its nearest community center again. We keep doing this until the community centres converge after a few iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Geodesic 2-medoids clustering: assign nodes to the nearest of two centers, recompute centers, repeat.

nodes.name: Local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary
nodes.statement:
\mypar{Dictionary Representations}
We collect local sets by level in
ascending order in a dictionary, with atoms corresponding to each
local set, that is, $ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC} = \{ {\bf 1}_{S_{i, j}} \}_{i=0, j = 1}^{i=T, j = 2^i}$.
We call it the~\emph{local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary}.

nodes.name: Local-set-based wavelet basis vector
Local-set-based wavelet basis in matrix form
nodes.statement:
To represent in a matrix form, the wavelet basis is
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC} = \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC} \mathrm{D}_2,
\end{eqnarray*}
where the downsampling matrix
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \mathrm{D}_2 & = &
 \begin{bmatrix}
 \frac{1}{\left\| \mathbf{d}_1 \right\|_2} & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & \phantom{+} g(\mathbf{d}_2, \mathbf{d}_3)  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & -g(\mathbf{d}_3, \mathbf{d}_2)  & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
  0 & \phantom{+}0 & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 0 & \phantom{+}0   & \cdots & \phantom{+}0 \\
 \vdots & \phantom{+}\vdots & \ddots & \phantom{+}\vdots \\
  0 & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & \phantom{+}g(\mathbf{d}_{2N-2}, \mathbf{d}_{2N-1} )  \\
 0 & \phantom{+}0  & \cdots & -g(\mathbf{d}_{2N-1}, \mathbf{d}_{2N-2}) \\
 \end{bmatrix}
 \\
 & \in  & \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{(2N-1) \times N},
\end{eqnarray*}
with $\mathbf{d}_i$ is the $i$th column of $\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$, and 
 $$
 g(\mathbf{d}_i, \mathbf{d}_j) = \sqrt{ \frac{\left\| \mathbf{d}_j \right\|_0} { ( \left\| \mathbf{d}_i \right\|_0  + \left\| \mathbf{d}_j \right\|_0 ) \left\| \mathbf{d}_i \right\|_0  }}.
 $$
nodes.statement_short: W_LSPC = D_LSPC D_2, where D_2 combines and reweights pairs of sibling atoms.

nodes.name: Wavelet basis vectors on four nodes
Local-set-based Wavelet Basis Construction
nodes.statement:
\footnotesize
  \caption{ Local-set-based  Wavelet Basis Construction }
  \begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
    \addlinespace[1mm]
   {\bf Input} 
      & $G(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E}, \mathrm{A} )$~~graph \\
     {\bf Output}  
      & $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$~~~~~~wavelet basis \\
    \addlinespace[2mm]
    {\bf Function} & &\\
    & initialize a stack of node sets $\mathbb{S}$ and a set of vectors $\mathrm{W}$ \\
    & push $S = \mathcal{V}$ into $\mathbb{S}$ \\ 
    & add $\mathbf{w} = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{|S|}} {\bf 1}_S$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ \\
    & while the cardinality of the largest element of $\mathbb{S}$ is bigger than $1$  \\ 
    &~pop up one element from $\mathbb{S}$ as $S$ \\
    &~partition $S$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_1, S_2$ \\
    &~push $S_1, S_2$ into $\mathbb{S}$ \\
    &~add $\mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left(  \frac{1}{|S_1|} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{|S_2|} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right)$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$\\
    & end \\
    & {\bf return} $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ \\  
     \addlinespace[1mm]
  \end{tabular}
nodes.statement_short: Recursively split node sets into two connected sets, adding a normalized Haar-like vector per split.
nodes.label: alg:wavelet

nodes.name: Local sets satisfy the multiresolution analysis
nodes.statement: The proposed construction of local sets satisfies the multiresolution analysis on graphs.
conclusions: The proposed construction of local sets satisfies the multiresolution analysis on graphs.
nodes.label: thm:MRA

nodes.name: Finer local sets are less smooth
conclusions: A series of local sets with a finer resolution is less smooth
nodes.label: thm:smooth

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement:
We first show that the sum of variations of two children local sets is larger than the variation of the parent local set.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j-1}) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j})  
\\
& = & \frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j-1}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + 
\frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} } \right\|_0
\\
& \stackrel{(a)}{ \geq } &  \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| }  \left(  \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} }  \right\|_0 \right)
\\
& \stackrel{(b)}{\geq} &  \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}} \right\|_0 \ = \ \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0}  (S_{i,j}),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $(a)$ follows from that the cardinality of the the parent local set is larger than either of its children local sets and $(b)$ follows from that we need to cut a boundary to partition two children local sets. Since every local set in the $i$th level has two children local sets in the $i+1$th level and every local set in the $i+1$th level has a parent local set in the $i$th local, we sum them together and obtain Theorem~\ref{thm:smooth}.
nodes.statement_short: Children variations exceed the parent's (smaller sets, extra cut edges); sum over levels.

nodes.name: Local-set-based wavelet basis is orthonormal
nodes.statement: The local-set-based wavelet basis constructs an orthonormal basis.
conclusions: The local-set-based wavelet basis constructs an orthonormal basis.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 8
nodes.statement:
First, we show each vector has norm one.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \left\| \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left(  \frac{1}{ | S_1 |} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{| S_2 |} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right)  \right\|_2^2 
\\
&  \stackrel{(a)}{=} & 
|S_1|  \left( \sqrt{\frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}}  \frac{1}{ | S_1 |}  \right)^2 +  |S_2|  \left( \sqrt{\frac{|S_1| |S_1|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}}  \frac{1}{ | S_2 |}  \right)^2 
\\
& = & 1,
\end{eqnarray*}
where $(a)$ follows from that $S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset$.
Second, we show each vector is orthogonal to the other vectors. We have
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\bf 1}^T \mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left( \sum_{i \in S_1} \frac{1}{ | S_1 |}  -  \sum_{i \in S_2} \frac{1}{| S_2 |}  \right) = 0.
\end{eqnarray*}
Thus, each vector is orthogonal to the first vector, ${\bf 1}_{\mathcal{V}}/\sqrt{|{\mathcal{V}}| }$. Each other individual vector is generated from two node sets. Let $S_1, S_2$ generate $\mathbf{w}_i$ and $S_3, S_4$ generate $\mathbf{w}_j$. Due to the construction, there are only two conditions, two node sets of one vector belongs to one node set of the other vector, and all four node sets do not share element with each other. For the first case, without losing generality, let $\left( S_3 \cup S_4 \right) \cap S_1=  S_3 \cup S_4$, we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \mathbf{w}_i^T \mathbf{w}_j 
& = &  \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}
 \frac{|S_3| |S_4|}{|S_3|+|S_4|}} \left( \sum_{i \in S_3} \frac{1}{ | S_3 |}  -  \sum_{i \in S_4} \frac{1}{| S_4 |} \right) 
\\ 
& = & 0.
\end{eqnarray*}
For the second case, the inner product between  $\mathbf{w}_i$ and $\mathbf{w}_j $ is zero because their supports do not match.
Third, we show that $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$ spans $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^N$. Since we recursively partition the node set until the cardinalities of all the node sets are smaller than 2, there are $N$ vectors in $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$.
nodes.statement_short: Check unit norm, pairwise orthogonality by nesting/disjointness of supports, and count N vectors.

nodes.name: Local-set-based wavelet basis promotes sparsity
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the output of Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} and $T$ be the maximum level of the decomposition in Algorithm~\ref{alg:wavelet} .
nodes.statement_short: Wavelet coefficients have at most T times as many nonzeros as the number of inconsistent edges.
nodes.label: thm:sparse

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9
nodes.statement_short: Counting: each edge is activated by at most one basis vector per level, so at most T in total.

nodes.name: Even partition gives the best sparsity
nodes.statement: The maximum level of the decomposition is determined by the choice of graph partition algorithm. Theorem~\ref{thm:sparse} shows that what it matters is the cardinality of each local set, instead of the shape of each local set. To achieve the best sparse representation, we should partition each local set as evenly as possible. Note that when the partition is perfectly even, the resulting wavelet basis is the same with the classical Haar wavelet basis.

nodes.name: Sparsity of the local-set-based piecewise-constant dictionary
nodes.label: thm:sparse

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1 (in prose)
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{W}$ is obtained from $ \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPC}$,  the worst case is to represent $\mathbf{x}$ by using $\mathrm{W}$.
nodes.statement_short: Each wavelet vector is a combination of two dictionary atoms, so the wavelet expansion is a worst case.

nodes.name: Sparsity under even partition
assumptions: Let the local-set-based wavelet basis evenly partition the node set each time.

nodes.name: Optimality of the even-partition local-set-based wavelet basis
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{W}$ be the local-set-based wavelet basis with the even partition.
nodes.statement_short: The even-partition wavelet basis minimizes the worst-case sparsity over orthonormal bases for K-cut piecewise-constant signals.

nodes.name: Difference operator versus wavelet basis
nodes.statement: In general, the graph difference operator provides more sparse representation than the local-set-based wavelet basis, however, the graph difference operator is not necessarily a one-to-one mapping and is bad at reconstruction; the graph difference operator only focuses on the pairwise relationship. On the other hand, the local-set-based wavelet basis is good at reconstruction and provides multiresolution view in the graph vertex domain.

nodes.name: Even partition is not always preferable
nodes.statement: The even partition minimizes the worst case; it does not necessarily mean that the even partition is good for all the applications. For example, a graph has two communities, a huge one and a tiny one, which hints that a piecewise-constant graph signal sits on a part of either of two communities. In this case, we cut a few edges to partition two communities and assign a local set for each of them, instead of partitioning the huge community to make sure that two local sets have a same cardinality.

nodes.statement:
We collect the sub-dictionaries for all the multiresolution local sets to form the~\emph{local-set-based piecewise-smooth dictionary}, that is,

nodes.name: Sparsity of the local-set-based piecewise-smooth dictionary
nodes.statement:
For all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PBL}_{\mathrm{V}_L}(C,K)$, where $\mathrm{V}_L$ is the graph Fourier basis of the graph Laplacian matrix $\mathrm{L}$,   we have $\left\| \mathbf{a}^* \right\|_0 \leq  2 K T\left\|  \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}} \right\|_0$, where $T$ is the maximum level of the decomposition, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}}$ is a piecewise-constant signal that corresponds the same local sets with $\mathbf{x}$ and
\begin{eqnarray*}
   \mathbf{a}^* &  = &   \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}}   \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0,
   \\
   && {\rm subject~to~}  \left\| \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS} \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2 \leq \epsilon_{\rm par}  \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2,
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\epsilon_{\rm par} $ is a constant determined by graph partitioning.
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise-bandlimited signals are approximated within eps_par by at most 2KT||Delta x_PC||_0 atoms of D_LSPS.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement:
The main idea is that we approximate a bandlimited signal in the original graph by using bandlimited signals in subgraphs. Based on the eigenvectors of graph Laplacian matrix, we define the bandlimited space, where each signal can be represented as $\mathbf{x} = \mathrm{V}_{(K)} \mathbf{a},$ where $\mathrm{V}_{(K)}$ is the submatrix of $\mathrm{V}$ containing the first $K$ columns in $\mathrm{V}$. We can show that this bandlimited space is a subspace of the total pairwise smooth space $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \leq  \lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} \}$. 

\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} 
\  = \  \sum_{i,j \in \mathcal{E}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2
\\
& = & \sum_{S_c} \sum_{i,j \in \mathcal{E}_{S_c}} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2  + \sum_{i,j \in (\mathcal{E} / \cup_{c} \mathcal{E}_{S_c}) } \mathrm{W}_{i,j} (x_i - x_j)^2
\\
& = &  \sum_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} + \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x} \ \leq \    \lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x},
\end{eqnarray*}
where $\mathrm{L}_{S_c}$ is the graph Laplacian matrix of the subgraph $G_{S_c}$ and  $\mathrm{L}_{S_c}$ stores the residual edges, which are cut in the graph partition algorithm.


Thus, $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L} \mathbf{x} \leq  \lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} \}$ is a subset of $\bigcup_{S_c}  \{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq  \lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x}  \}$; that is, any  total pairwise smooth graph signal in the whole graph can be precisely represented by total pairwise smooth graph signals in the subgraphs.

In each local set, when we use the bandlimited space 
$\{ \mathbf{x}: \mathbf{x} = {\mathrm{V}_{S_c}}_{(K)} \mathbf{a} \}$ to approximate the space $\{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq   c \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \}$, the maximum error we suffer from is $c \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x}_{S_c} / \lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$, which is solved by the following optimization problem,
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&	\max_{\mathbf{x}}  \left\|  \mathbf{x} - \mathrm{V}_{S_c} \mathrm{V}_{S_c}^T \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2
	\\
&&	{\rm subject~to:}~   \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x} \leq   c  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}.
\end{eqnarray*}
In other words, in each local set, the maximum error to represent $ \{\mathbf{x}_{S_c}: \mathbf{x}_{S_c}^T \mathrm{L}_{S_c} \mathbf{x}_{S_c} \leq  \lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x}   \}$ is 
$(\lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x})/\lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$. Since all the local sets share the variation budget of $\lambda_K \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x}$ together, the maximum error we suffer from is $\epsilon_{\rm par} \left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2^2 = (\lambda_K  \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T \mathrm{L}_{\rm cut} \mathbf{x})/ \min_{S_c} \lambda^{(S_c)}_{K+1}$.



In Theorem~\ref{thm:sparse}, we have shown that we need at most $2 T \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{PC}} \right\|_0$ local sets to represent the piecewise-constant template of $\mathbf{x}$. Since we use at most $K$ eigenvectors in each local set, we obtain the results in Theorem~\ref{thm:PPL}.
nodes.statement_short: Split the Laplacian quadratic form over local sets and cut edges, bound each local bandlimited approximation error, then count local sets via Corollary 1.

nodes.name: Detection of piecewise-smooth signals with the LSPS dictionary
nodes.statement:
We consider statistically testing the null and alternative hypothesis,
\begin{eqnarray*}
H_0 &:& \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 \mathrm{I}), 
\\
H_1 &:&  \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}, \sigma^2 \mathrm{I}),~\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PBL}_{\mathrm{V}_L}(C,K).
\end{eqnarray*}
We solve the following optimization problem
\begin{eqnarray*}
   \mathbf{a}_{\mathbf{y}}^* &  = &   \arg \min_{\mathbf{a}}  \left\| \mathbf{y} - \mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS} \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2   
   \\
   && {\rm subject~to~}  \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_0 \leq 2KT  \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\rm PC} \right\|_0,
\end{eqnarray*}
by using the matching pursuit algorithm. We reject the null if $\left\| \mathbf{a}_{\mathbf{y}}^* \right\|_{\infty} > \tau$. Set $\tau = \sigma \sqrt{2 \log(KNT/\delta)}$. If
$$
\frac{\left\| \mathbf{x} \right\|_2}{\sigma} \geq C \sqrt{2KT \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\rm PC} \right\|_0 }  \sqrt{8 \log(\frac{KNT}{\delta})},
$$
where $C = \max_{ |\Omega| \leq 2KT \left\| \Delta \mathbf{x}_{\rm PC} \right\|_0  } \left\| (\mathrm{D}_{\rm LSPS})_{\Omega} \right\|_2 /(1- \sqrt{\epsilon_{\rm par}}) $. Then under $H_0$, $\mathbb{P}({\rm Reject}) \leq \delta$, and under $H_1$, $\mathbb{P} ({\rm Reject}) \leq \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Thresholding the sparse-coding coefficients over D_LSPS detects piecewise-bandlimited signals with error at most delta above an SNR level.
nodes.label: thm:PPL_Detect

nodes.name: Pairwise bound
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{PL}(1)$, that is,
$$
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}

$$
Then, we write the pairwise Lipschitz smooth criterion as
\begin{eqnarray*}
|x_i - x_j| 
& = &  | \sum_{k} \left( d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) \right)   a_k |
\\
& \leq &  \sum_{k} | d(v_k, v_i) - d(v_k, v_j) |  |a_k |
\\
\\
& \leq &  \sum_{k} |a_k |  | d(v_i, v_j) | \ = \ \left\| \mathbf{a} \right\|_1  | d(v_i, v_j) |.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand x in PL(1) and bound |x_i - x_j| by the triangle inequality

nodes.name: Pointwise bound
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be a graph signal with bandwidth $K$, that is,
$$
\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k,
$$
Then, we write the local normalized neighboring smooth criterion as

\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \left| x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} }  \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j  \right|
\\
&= &   \left| \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_i - \sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} \left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k \right)_j \right|
\\
& = &   \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k \left(  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{P}_{i,j} (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_j \right) \right|
\\
& = &   \left| \sum_{k=1}^{K} \widehat{x}_k  (1 - \lambda_k)  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i \right|
\\
& \leq &  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})  \left| \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \widehat{x}_k  (\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k)_i  \right| \ = \  (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})  |x_i|.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Pointwise bound of the local deviation by (1 - lambda_K)|x_i|

nodes.name: Sum of squares
nodes.statement:
The last equality follows from the fact that $\mathbf{v}^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ and $\lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_k$ are eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $\mathrm{P}$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \sum_i \left(  x_i -  \frac{1}{\sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i }}  \sum_{j  \in \mathcal{N}_i } \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j  \right)^2 
\\
& = & \sum_{i=1}^{N} |x_i - \frac{1}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} }  \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i} \mathrm{W}_{i,j} x_j |^2
\\
& \leq & \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}   (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K} )^2  |x_i|^2 \ = \   (1 - \lambda^{(\mathrm{P})}_{K})^2 .
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Justify via eigen-relation and sum squares to get (1 - lambda_K)^2

nodes.name: Upper bound
nodes.statement:
We first show $\left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega}  \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma} \right\|_2 \leq \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}  \sqrt{ |\Gamma|\cdot |\Omega|}$.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&	( \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma}  \mathbf{x} )_s
\ = \ \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \left( \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} x_i \right)
\\
& = &  \sum_{i \in \Gamma}  \left(   \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} \right) x_i
\ = \ \sum_i q(s,i) x_i,
\end{eqnarray*}
   where
   \begin{equation*} q(s,i) = 
  \left\{ 
    \begin{array}{rl}
      \sum_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{V}_{s,k} \mathrm{U}_{k,i}, & i \in \Gamma;\\
      0, & \mbox{otherwise}.
  \end{array} \right.
\end{equation*}
Let $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$ be a graph signal with $y^{(i)}_s = q(s,i)$. Then, $( \widehat{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}} )_k = {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{U}_{k,i}$. We then have
\begin{eqnarray*}
&&	\left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma}  \right\|_{2}^2
 \ \leq \  \left\| \mathrm{V}_{\Omega} \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \mathrm{I}_{\Gamma}  \right\|_{\rm HS}^2
\\
& = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{s} |q(s,i)|^2 
\ =  \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \mathbf{y}^{(i)} \right\|_2^2
\\
& = & \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \left\| \widehat{ \mathbf{y}^{(i)} } \right\|_2^2
\ = \  \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} \left( {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} \mathrm{U}_{k,i} \right)^2
\\
& \leq & \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 \sum_{i \in \Gamma} \sum_{k} {\bf 1}_{k \in \Omega} 
\ = \   \left\| \mathrm{U}_{\Omega} \right\|_{\infty}^2 |\Gamma| \cdot |\Omega|.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Upper-bound ||V_Omega U_Omega I_Gamma|| via the Hilbert-Schmidt norm

nodes.name: Parent-child inequality
nodes.statement:
We first show that the sum of variations of two children local sets is larger than the variation of the parent local set.
\begin{eqnarray*}
&& \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j-1}) + \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0} (S_{i+1,2j})  
\\
& = & \frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j-1}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + 
\frac{1}{ |S_{i+1,2j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} } \right\|_0
\\
& \stackrel{(a)}{ \geq } &  \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| }  \left(  \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j-1} } \right\|_0 + \left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{ S_{i+1,2j} }  \right\|_0 \right)
\\
& \stackrel{(b)}{\geq} &  \frac{1}{ |S_{i,j}| }\left\| \Delta {\bf 1}_{S_{i,j}} \right\|_0 \ = \ \mathrm{S}_{\Delta, 0}  (S_{i,j}),
\end{eqnarray*}
where $(a)$ follows from that the cardinality of the the parent local set is larger than either of its children local sets and $(b)$ follows from that we need to cut a boundary to partition two children local sets.
nodes.statement_short: Children's variations dominate the parent's

nodes.statement: Under the null, we have $\left\| \mathbf{a}_{\mathbf{e}}^* \right\|_{\infty} < \sigma \sqrt{2 \log( KNT /\delta)}$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. We set $\tau = \sigma \sqrt{2 \log(KNT/\delta)}$ to control the type 1 error.
nodes.statement_short: Type 1 error control by Gaussian maximum

nodes.name: Alternative
nodes.statement_short: Type 2 error control via Theorem 11

nodes.name: Initialize root
nodes.statement_short: Root set is the whole node set

nodes.name: First split
nodes.statement_short: First bipartition gives V_1

nodes.name: Recurse
nodes.statement:
We then
recursively partition each larger local set into two smaller local
sets.
nodes.statement_short: Recurse on each set

nodes.name: Level split
nodes.statement_short: Level-i split of each S_{i,j}

nodes.name: Stop
nodes.statement:
When
$|S_{i,j}| \leq 1$, $S_{i+1,2j-1} = S_{i,j}$ and $S_{i+1,2j} =
\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Stop splitting singletons

nodes.name: Fiedler vector
nodes.statement: We first obtain the graph Laplacian matrix of a local set and compute the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of the graph Laplacian matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Fiedler vector of the local Laplacian

nodes.name: Threshold
nodes.statement: We then set the median number of the eigenvector as the threshold;
nodes.statement_short: Median threshold

nodes.name: Split
nodes.statement: we put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are no smaller than the threshold into a children local set and put the nodes whose corresponding values in the eigenvector are smaller than the threshold into the other children local set.
nodes.statement_short: Split by threshold

nodes.name: Spanning tree
nodes.statement: we first obtain the maximum spanning tree of the subgraph
nodes.statement_short: Maximum spanning tree

nodes.name: Balance node
nodes.statement: then find a balance node in the spanning tree.
nodes.statement_short: Balance node

nodes.name: Split
nodes.statement: We remove the balance node from the spanning tree, the resulting largest connected component form a children local set and the other nodes including the balance node forms the other children local set.
nodes.statement_short: Split at balance node

nodes.name: Init centers
nodes.statement: We first randomly select 2 nodes as the community center and assign every other node to its nearest community center based on the geodesic distance.
nodes.statement_short: Random centers and assignment

nodes.name: Update
nodes.statement: We then recompute the community center for each community by minimizing the summation of the geodesic distances to all the other nodes in the community and assign node to its nearest community center again.
nodes.statement_short: Recompute medoids and reassign

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: We keep doing this until the community centres converge after a few iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate to convergence

nodes.name: Initialize
nodes.statement: initialize a stack of node sets $\mathbb{S}$ and a set of vectors $\mathrm{W}$
nodes.statement_short: Empty stack and basis

nodes.name: Push root
nodes.statement: push $S = \mathcal{V}$ into $\mathbb{S}$
nodes.statement_short: Push whole node set

nodes.name: Constant vector
nodes.statement: add $\mathbf{w} = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{|S|}} {\bf 1}_S$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$
nodes.statement_short: Add the normalized constant vector

nodes.name: Main loop
nodes.statement:
while the cardinality of the largest element of $\mathbb{S}$ is bigger than $1$  \\ 
    &~pop up one element from $\mathbb{S}$ as $S$ \\
    &~partition $S$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_1, S_2$ \\
    &~push $S_1, S_2$ into $\mathbb{S}$ \\
    &~add $\mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left(  \frac{1}{|S_1|} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{|S_2|} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right)$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$
nodes.statement_short: Loop while some set has more than one node

nodes.name: Pop
nodes.statement: pop up one element from $\mathbb{S}$ as $S$
nodes.statement_short: Pop a set

nodes.name: Partition
nodes.statement: partition $S$ into two disjoint connected sets $S_1, S_2$
nodes.statement_short: Partition with a graph partition algorithm

nodes.name: Push children
nodes.statement: push $S_1, S_2$ into $\mathbb{S}$
nodes.statement_short: Push children

nodes.name: Wavelet vector
nodes.statement: add $\mathbf{w} = \sqrt{ \frac{|S_1| |S_2|}{|S_1|+|S_2|}} \left(  \frac{1}{|S_1|} {\bf 1}_{S_1} - \frac{1}{|S_2|} {\bf 1}_{S_2}\right)$ into $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$
nodes.statement_short: Add the Haar-like wavelet vector

nodes.name: Return
nodes.statement: {\bf return} $\mathrm{W}_{\rm LSPC}$
nodes.statement_short: Return the basis

nodes.name: Partition
nodes.statement: Instead of obtaining a full decomposition tree, we partition the local sets until we obtain $m$ leaf local sets.
nodes.statement_short: Partition until m leaf sets

nodes.name: Order
nodes.statement: For the local sets in the same level of the decomposition tree, we first partition the one that has the largest number of nodes.
nodes.statement_short: Split largest set first

nodes.name: Centers
nodes.statement: For each leaf local set, we choose a center that has the minimum summation of the geodesic distances to all the other nodes in the leaf local set.
nodes.statement_short: Geodesic center of each leaf set

nodes.name: Sample
nodes.statement: We use those centers for the $M$  leaf local sets as the sampled set.
nodes.statement_short: Centers form the sample set

nodes.name: Recover
nodes.statement_short: Assign each sample's value to its leaf set
